There’s a sort of irony that, despite being a beyond exceptional technical directing talent who only gained the assistance of even more exceptional technical directing talent along the way, Iñárritu is by far the most graceless, hollow showboater Hollywood has seen in decades, arguably even more than someone as derided for showboating as Michael Bay. He’s a monkey’s paw curse made man: born with both divine technical ability and the worst possible thematic and narrative instincts those technical abilities could be paired with. Derivative, overly-literal macho faux-art nonsense. Historically irresponsible, burdened with clunky attempts at spiritualist visual metaphor and just way, waaaaaay too long. Lubezki can light and shoot snow-covered forests and babbling brooks all day but he can’t save a movie that, at its core, has nothing of any worth to say. Nothing truly relevant or engaging happens between those beautifully composed frames, save for a final shot that attempts to add deeper subtext the narrative itself does not attempt to possess. If you're after a “man fights nature/masculinity” movie set in a lot of snowy forest wildernesses that’s actually good, Joe Carnahan’s “The Grey” is a daring masterpiece.

Leonardo DiCaprio gehört zweifelsohne zu den besten  US-amerikanischen Schauspielern der Gegenwart. Lange musste er trotz einer beeindruckenden Filmografie auf den längst verdienten Oscar als Bester Haupdarsteller warten. Umso trauriger, dass er mit diesem für  den Rachewestern "The Revenant" ausgezeichnet wurde. Von der großartigen Schauspielkunst DiCaprios ist hier hinter seinem Bart und unter dem Schnee leider wenig zu sehen. Seine Leinwandkollegen Tom Hardy oder die Grizzlybärin können diesen auch nicht übertreffen. Der von DiCaprio verkörperte Hugh Glass und der Pferdekadaver sind auch kein gutes Leinwandpaar. Dass DiCaprio sowie Regiesseur Alejandro González Iñárritu für diesen Film jeweils mit dem Oscar ausgezeichnet wurden, bestätigt noch einmal die Blut, Schweiß und Tränen-Ideologie der Academy.  Survival-Challenges oder dass man als Vegetarier rohe Bisonleber verspeist, scheinen wohl Merkmale guter Schauspielkunst zu sein. Es wirkt, als sei dieser Film vor allem gemacht worden, um bei der Oscarverleihung 2016 abzuräumen. Sieht man mal von den Schauspielern ab, hat der Film weder oberflächlich noch inhaltlich etwas zu bieten. Die Handlung ist banal und die Landschaftsaufnahmen erinnern eher an den Windows-Sperrbildschirm als an großes Western-Kino. Die Suche nach Spiritualität wirkt aufgesetzt, um der Handlung künstlich Tiefe zu verleihen. Es hätte ja ein interessanter Film sein können, der das Verhältnis von Mensch und Natur und die Themen und Fragen des Western-Genres aufgreift und neu verhandelt. Doche solche Fragen und Genre-Motive sind hier eher lose Assoziationen als bedeutungstragende Elemente des Films. Möglicherweise wird "The Revenant" nur dafür in Erinnerung bleiben, dass Leonardo DiCaprio für diesen Film seinen bisher einzigen Oscar als Bester Hauptdarsteller gewann.

J’ai surtout eu l’impression d’admirer la réalisation plutôt que de réellement vivre l’histoire avec les personnages. Un film très bien réalisé et impressionnant visuellement, mais qui ne m’a malheureusement pas autant marqué que je l’espérais.

A história de Hugh Glass , por ter resistido ao ataque de um urso-pardo, ter sido abandonado para morrer por seus próprios companheiros e ter sobrevivido por dias sozinho no meio do nada, já seria suficientemente interessante para carregar a história de um filme por si só. Mas, para as pessoas envolvidas nessa obra, aparentemente, não era. Eles precisavam fazer com que a história desse americano branco invasor de terras de alguma forma se relacionasse com uma cultura minoritária com a qual ele nunca teve envolvimento direto. Tudo que envolve os personagens nativos nessa trama é utilizado única e exclusivamente como palanque para criar algum tipo de drama ou objetivo que de alguma forma engrandeça o protagonista e “justifique” ele tomar essa história envolvendo cultura uma cultura que ele não faz parte de assalto, terminando o filme como o grande herói dela. A esposa nativa morta por soldados americanos? Nunca existiu . O filho assassinado na sua frente e que serve como o combustível por trás de toda essa vingança? Nunca existiu , na verdade, o combustível de toda essa jornada foi poder empunhar seu rifle mais uma vez (bem mais adequado para quem a figura realmente foi). O personagem nativo que o ajuda no momento mais oportuno e conveniente e depois é cruelmente assassinado para novamente ser usado como escada para o arco de Glass? Nunca existiu . Ou então toda a subtrama envolvendo a filha do líder Arikara resgatada pelo nosso grande herói? Também nunca existiu . Basicamente, qualquer relação entre o personagem principal e qualquer elemento da cultura nativa nunca existiu, mesmo que aqui ele seja representado quase como o Superman dessa minoria. Esse arquétipo narrativo do “ White Savior Trope” (o tropo do salvador branco) não é algo novo no cinema ocidental, na verdade, o que mais tem são filmes sobre culturas e minorias menosprezadas pelo branco americano/europeu médio que de alguma forma acaba sendo retratado como seu salvador. Mas quem dera esse fosse o único problema desse filme. Além de embranquecer tudo o que pode, O Regresso é um filme totalmente sem ritmo , pretensioso , prolixo e muitas vezes apenas entediante mesmo. A maior força dele está nas cenas de ação, que até são bem filmadas, mas principalmente na forma como ele consegue captar toda essa brutalidade que um filme de sobrevivência precisa ter. Fora isso, é um filme que anda, anda, anda e parece não sair do lugar. E, para rechear essa história de quase três horas de duração, acaba entupindo-a de subtramas e dramas que são completamente jogados, mal desenvolvidos e com os quais no fundo ninguém se importa. O filme não consegue sequer criar uma relação convincente entre um pai e um filho assassinado na sua frente, quem dirá uma trama realmente interessante e instigante . Na busca por sua primeira estatueta, o Leonardo DiCaprio até que realmente entrega uma boa atuação, mesmo achando que ele já poderia ter vencido essa premiação até mesmo antes desse papel. Mas, em busca de um grande épico, rechaçado pela crítica e cheio de glamour com assuntos raciais e camadas profundas, o diretor Iñárritu acaba entregando apenas uma experiência historicamente ofensiva , tediosa e arrastada , que se resume a uma ou outra sequência que realmente se salva. No fim das contas, se tem alguém que merecia ganhar um prêmio com esse filme somos eu e você, que conseguimos aguentar estas quase três horas de tédio e “ whitewashing ”. O Oscar de espectador mais resiliente do ano vai para... VOCÊ .

The script is simple: revenge after injustice. The movie is built around the pain and suffering of Hugh Glass, who has his stepson killed by Fitzgerald after their settlement is attacked by Native Americans. A premise like that demands great performances to make an impact, and that's what holds the entire movie together. DiCaprio delivers it pretty well. It isn't one of his best performances, but it's a good one. Unpopular opinion: I believe Tom Hardy is the standout of the entire film! I don't usually expect much from him, and that's exactly why his performance is so impressive. Maybe the best character he has ever played. The whole time he is on screen, he grabs your attention. Simply as that. We've all seen dozens of revenge movies, but DiCaprio and, mainly, Hardy make this one stand out. The direction is great, and the scenes are raw, bloody, and aggressive. The soundtrack is subtle but works well. In short: the movie is simple, well-paced, and well-structured, and Hardy's performance makes it even cooler. OBS: DiCaprio has played several characters better than this one. It's kind of sad that "The Revenant" was the role that finally won him the award in 2016.

I did it! I watched The Revenant! What did I get out of the experience, you ask? First things first: Naughty Dog and Rockstar should be bending their knees to Iñárritu after ripping off their respective climactic fights from this film. The Revenant: probably in the upper echelon of "films I've never seen despite my age and preferences in actors and Oscar history." I remember watching the commercials before its release, but I was too young at the time to go see it (or at least too young to want to witness Leo crawl into the belly of a stallion). I have fond memories of the "Leo has never won an Oscar" memes, and endlessly watched WatchMojo's incessantness in crowning him in the number one spot for Oscarless movie stars. Despite my desire, the half-face Leo staring into the lens of the camera poster never caught my eye enough on streaming services to warrant a click (the 150-minute runtime doesn't help either, but this is also the guy who watched Oppenheimer 6 times, so take that claim with a grain of salt). Thank god HBO Max decided to blow the dust off of their Digger-related media this month. I've already watched Birdman, and I've started The Last Samurai (which doesn't look to be passing the Woke-ometer based on the first half hour). I'm taking the opportunity given to me and consuming myself with all the knowledge I can before the first of next month, when my most anticipated movie of the year comes out (It's Verity). A decade of buildup, the final episode when I finally watch the movie- does it live up to the hype I've built up in my mind... Um... Eh. Remember in The Last Jedi when they act like they're going to kill off Leia, and give her this really beautiful swan song scene, only to have her survive the attack and then never speak again throughout the rest of the trilogy. Like, yeah, that was all good and dandy, but what's the point? That's how I feel about The Revenant. Sure, Leo gives a great performance, the camera work is electric, and the cinematography is beautiful, but what does any of it amount to other than meeting those specified criteria? Why does The Revenant exist? Is it commenting on some greater cultural theme that 2015 audiences could resonate with? I don't see any. Is it trying to be an Odyssey-esque revenge story for Leo to shine in? I guess, but it doesn't do anything particularly unique besides replacing the Cyclops with a bear. I just see no reason for this movie to exist other than to watch people's eyes open in bewildered awe as you explain to them the basic plot points of the film. Happy for Leo, worried about Digger.

Revisiting this almost ten years after I first reviewed it, and my impression hasn't budged: same admiration, same reservations, same grade. This is a film that demands something from you, and the rewatch was every bit as punishing as I remembered. Not a flaw, a design. The cold, the length, the sheer physical exhaustion of Glass dragging himself back to life all become something you endure rather than simply watch. On the technical side it is close to flawless. Iñárritu's direction is staggering, and Lubezki shooting on nothing but natural light gives you images you don't forget. DiCaprio throws his whole body into a nearly wordless role and finally got the Oscar he'd been chasing, with Tom Hardy just as good as the treacherous Fitzgerald. The lifelike makeup seals the immersion. Everything you can point a camera at, or build in front of one, is working at the highest level. Where it falls short is the script. The pacing sags in stretches, and too many scenes seem to exist for their visual force rather than any real narrative weight, beauty that doesn't always serve the whole. It's a monumental thing to behold and a hard one to sit through, and I respect it more than I love it. A survival epic that earns its greatness and makes you pay for every minute of it.

The Revenant is among the most beautiful and aesthetically pleasing movies I’ve ever seen combined with excellently written characters. It’s a compelling setting and premise for a 1820s frontier showcase of sorts, relying on the environment to carry much of the movie. My only downside is that at times the story is extremely basic as it builds up Hugh Glass (Leonardo DiCaprio) post bear scene. Where it relies on mostly heavy breathing and silence to carry more emotional dialogue scenes in typical films, it’s so out of the box for a blockbuster that it’s oddly soothing. Seeing Hugh go from death to the bring of triumph was beautiful storytelling, with some good family connections and tie ins to the beginning scenes. Leo was absolutely spectacular in this movie, deserving of that Oscar for sure, but he also had one of the most complete characters in recent filmmaking. For as great as Leo was is as uninspired I found the rest of the cast highlighted by Tom Hardy as John Fitzgerald. Another great villain character written extremely well but for half of the film Hardy is mumbling and incoherent, maybe that’s the trick but it’s similar to how I felt watching Gary Oldman as Winston Churchill in Darkest Hour ; great character with a less than desirable performance. It took a while for me to truly understand the story, I wasn’t feeling the Hugh and Hawk (Forrest Goodluck) story, they spent so much time focusing on Hugh that Hawk isn’t given the proper depth to be a compelling character in his death. When they connect Hawk as the bridge for Hugh’s ultimate revenge on death being to see his wife again there’s layers to the characters that make a more compelling story. Funny enough it’s similar to how Inception felt with Leo and the wife underlining motive but on completely different ends of the isle. Even if the story isn’t my cup of horse blood the special effects, CGI, and landscape are so well done that it elevates the simple moments into can’t miss items. Seeing the wide shot landscape scenes of Hugh walking or sitting down pondering make the tension feel more important but the task more daunting than any dialogue could have done. It’s a completely different movie than I expected it to be, in having the main character mostly silent it needs strength in other ways which I’m glad they highlighted in his soft spoken nature and physicality. The detail work, especially on Hugh’s body, post bear battle scene changed the entire vibe of the movie into knowing this is legit something you haven’t seen before. I dug the entire environment, might not be something I watch again but definitely do recommend turning it on; it’s a beautiful movie with a poetic story with great moments and a solid overall execution.

Wow. C’est horrible à regarder (au sens figuré). Le film est incroyable, une tension glaçante et une cruauté sans précédent. C’est le plus grand film de vengeance que j’ai vu et fait partie des meilleurs dans sa catégorie sans aucun doute. Le jeu d’acteur de Dicaprio et Tom Hardy est juste phénoménal avec un Dicaprio qui joue parfaitement le lépreux revanchard et Tom Hardy qui joue le parfait connard narcissique et lâche. Qui a aucun moment, ne se remet en question sur les atrocités qu’il a commis car il agirait pour le bien seul de sa survie. Le film se passe dans un environnement terrifiant en plein dans les montagnes enneigées, ce qui donne un côté très horrifique et par conséquent très Shining à l’œuvre. La première heure du film et les derniers trois quarts d’heure sont du pur bonheur. En revanche je trouve le milieu du film un peu trop long. En effet 2h20 aurait été parfait. La cruauté, le mensonge, la loyauté et l’honneur sont très bien mis au premier plan. Je suis un peu sceptique sur la fin, d’un côté c’est intéressant qu’on ne sache pas comment il finit après avoir fait sa vengeance mais en même temps le film se coupe sur DiCaprio brisant le 4eme mur… mouais. Tellement de scènes marquantes, la scène du grizzly est folle, le suicide de l’amérindien également, l’épopée dans la neige dans sa globalité est très bien même s’ils auraient pu la raccourcir et le combat de fin est génial. Après s’être fait enlever l’être le plus cher à ses yeux, Dicaprio laisse le destin s’occuper d’Hardy malgré les atrocités qu’il a commis et sa volonté de le détruire. D’ailleurs les plans séquences sont incroyables ptn de merde, Iñarritu a fait un taf de malade mental (un chouïa plus lent et ce serait parfait car ça avait tendance à me faire un peu tourner la tête à la longue). This movie is so raw. It’s Leo stripped down to the absolute core, and he is so damn good. You feel his isolation, anger, grief, pain, and sheer will to survive without him having to say a word for damn near two hours. It’s pure acting at its core, where every look, breath, and movement tells you exactly what he is feeling. What makes it so good is how completely it pulls you into his suffering. The cold feels unbearable. The violence feels ugly and real. The silence makes everything feel even lonelier. Nothing feels polished or comfortable, and that makes every moment hit harder. The story is simple, but the execution makes it feel massive because you are watching a man get reduced to nothing except instinct, grief, and the need to keep moving. The cinematography and visuals are unbelievable. Every shot captures how devastating, brutal, and still beautiful the wilderness is. The natural lighting makes everything feel even more real, and the scale of the landscapes makes Hugh Glass feel completely insignificant against the world around him. It is one of those movies where the acting, direction, sound, and cinematography all work together so perfectly that you do not just watch it. You feel exhausted by the end of it. 93/100

I forgot how truly amazing The Revenant really is; I truly believe it’s a masterpiece. Leo gives one of the best performances of his career as Hugh Glass; he barely has any dialogue throughout the entire film, but he doesn’t need it. The way he portrays anger, grief and (above all) pain just from facial expressions and motion truly captures the horror his character goes through. Tom Hardy’s performance is the complete opposite; visually he’s almost completely emotionless, but he builds his sneering, disgusting character through how he delivers his dialogue. The film is visually stunning; the way AJI and Emmanuel Lubezki contrast the natural beauty of the frontier with the harsh brutality of living and going to war in such an environment, truly captures frontier life in 1820’s America. The brutality sticks out in particular in The Revenant ; the bear attack scene looks so real that it’s actually difficult to watch - Rachel was nearly in tears. The makeup and prosthetics applied to Leo, combined with his performance, seems so so genuine, and the fight between Hugh and Fitzgerald at the end feels so real and human and not choreographed at all (like when he axes his fingers off!!!). Some people say it’s slowwww, or boringgggg or poorly written but they’re all incredibly wrong. It’s a harrowing, brutally realistic tale of survival and revenge and I think it’s perfect.
